records.source: Ταῦτα ἐλάλησεν Ἰησοῦς, καὶ ἐπάρας τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν εἶπεν· Πάτερ, ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα· δόξασόν σου τὸν υἱόν, ἵνα ὁ υἱὸς δοξάσῃ σέ, καθὼς ἔδωκας αὐτῷ ἐξουσίαν πάσης σαρκός, ἵνα πᾶν ὃ δέδωκας αὐτῷ δώσῃ αὐτοῖς ζωὴν αἰώνιον.
records.gloss: These things spoke Jesus, and having lifted up the eyes of him to the heaven he said, "Father, has come the hour; glorify of you the Son, that the Son may glorify you, \v 2 just as you gave him authority of all flesh, that all that you have given him he may give to them life eternal.

L.1: Jesus spoke these things, and having lifted up {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} eyes to heaven, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "Father, the hour has come; glorify {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} Son, so that the Son may glorify {{deity_pronoun:you|You}},
L.2: just as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} authority over all flesh, so that all that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, to them {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} may give eternal life.

R.1: When Jesus had finished saying these things, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} looked up toward heaven and prayed. He said, "Father, the hour has come. Bring glory to {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} Son, so that the Son can bring glory to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.
R.2: You have put {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in charge of all people. You did this so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could give eternal life to all the people {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: the hour: the appointed time of Jesus's death and glorification, which has now arrived
alternatives: a period of time in general
decisions.reason: Through the Gospel Jesus's hour had not yet come (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). At 12:23 he said that it had come, and at 13:1 John calls it the hour to pass from this world to the Father. Here, at the start of his prayer, Jesus says it again to the Father: the cross, resurrection and return to the Father are at hand.

decisions.choice: glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you: the Father shows the Son's glory in the hour, and in that same event the Son shows the Father's
decisions.reason: Glorify is a key term. In John, Jesus is glorified when he is lifted up on the cross, raised, and returns to the Father (7:39; 12:23; 13:31-32). The glory of the two is bound together: when the Son is glorified, so is the Father (13:31-32; 14:13). Jesus's first request is not for his own sake alone but so that the Father may be honored.

decisions.choice: so that the Son may glorify you (SBLGNT)
alternatives: so that your Son also may glorify you (many later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "so that your Son also may glorify you", adding "also" and "your", which repeats the wording of the first request. The older manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, have the shorter text. The meaning is the same either way. A footnote gives the longer reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: authority over all flesh: authority over all human beings
decisions.reason: "All flesh" is a Hebrew way of speaking of all humankind, or of all living things (Genesis 6:12; Isaiah 40:5; Joel 2:28). Here the purpose clause that follows shows that people are meant: the authority is given so that the Son may give life. Compare the authority given to the Son to judge (5:27) and the Father giving all things into his hand (3:35).

decisions.choice: all that you have given him ... to them: the people given to the Son, seen first as one whole and then as persons
alternatives: all things that you have given him (things, not people)
decisions.reason: πᾶν ὃ is neuter, "all that": John speaks of all whom the Father gives as a single gift, as in 6:37 and 6:39. The sentence then turns to the plural masculine "to them", the persons who make up that gift. The neuter phrase stands first for emphasis and is taken up by "to them".

decisions.choice: just as: the gift of authority is the ground of the request
decisions.reason: καθὼς can compare ("just as") or give a reason ("since"). Here it does both: the Son asks to be glorified in keeping with what the Father has already given him, authority over all people, which has eternal life as its purpose.

decisions.choice: you, your, yours, yourself (to the Father); he, him, his, me, my (of the Son); in the whole prayer
decisions.reason: In this prayer Jesus speaks to the Father, so every "you" and "your" addressed to him uses the deity_pronoun setting, and so does every "me" and "my" with which Jesus speaks of himself and every "he" or "him" for the Son, as in 11:41-42. Plain "You" and "He" stand at the start of a sentence. The prayer runs to 17:26, so the quotation opened here does not close in this passage.

decisions.choice: all flesh, all that (L); all people, everyone (B); all people, all the people (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the idiom and the neuter. Balanced and Readable say what the idiom means (meaning decision m4) and use words for people where the Greek neuter means people (meaning decision m5), as 6:37 does. "All people" and "everyone" are already inclusive, so they need no gender setting.

decisions.choice: prayed (B, R); Bring glory to; put him in charge of; You did this so that
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly that what follows is a prayer, says "bring glory to" (as at 12:28), which keeps the key term in everyday speech, and splits the long sentence. "Hour" stays at every level, as at 12:23, so the thread through the Gospel stays visible.

records.heading: Jesus prays to be glorified

records.source: αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἡ αἰώνιος ζωὴ ἵνα γινώσκωσι σὲ τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν θεὸν καὶ ὃν ἀπέστειλας Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν.
records.gloss: This and is the eternal life, that they may know you the only true God and whom you sent, Jesus Christ.

L.3: And this is eternal life, that they may know {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, the only true God, and [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] whom {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent, Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.3: Eternal life means knowing {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, the only true God. It means knowing the one {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent, Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}.

decisions.choice: this is eternal life, that: the clause says what eternal life is
alternatives: this leads to eternal life, that they know
decisions.reason: "This" points forward to the clause that follows, which explains it, as in 6:29, 6:40 and 15:12. Eternal life is not only something that knowing God leads to; knowing God is what it consists of. Verse 2 spoke of the Son giving eternal life; this verse says what that life is.

decisions.choice: know: an ongoing, personal knowing, the knowing of a relationship
decisions.reason: γινώσκωσι is present tense: knowing that goes on, not a single act of learning. In the Bible to know God is to be in a living relationship with him, not only to know facts about him (Jeremiah 31:34; Hosea 6:6). Jesus speaks of the shepherd and the sheep knowing each other, as he and the Father know each other (10:14-15).

decisions.choice: the only true God, and the one he sent: the one God, known together with the Son he sent
decisions.reason: "The only true God" holds to the confession of Israel that there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4; compare 5:44). Beside him stands the one he sent, and knowing the Son belongs to the same eternal life. John keeps both truths together: there is one God, and the Son is with God and is God (1:1, 18; 10:30).

decisions.choice: Jesus Christ: Jesus names himself in the third person, with the full name, in the prayer
alternatives: Jesus's own words, a solemn naming of himself
John's own wording of the prayer
decisions.reason: The full name "Jesus Christ" occurs in this Gospel only here and at 1:17, and nowhere else does Jesus use it of himself. It is the way believers spoke of him after the resurrection. It may be that John, in giving the prayer, puts it in the words the church used, or Jesus may speak of himself in this solemn way as the one the Father sent. The text does not settle which. Christ is a title, "anointed one" (1:41).

decisions.choice: Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: As at 1:17, the title follows the name with the christos setting. The name stays at the end, as in the Greek, so the sentence closes on it.

decisions.choice: Eternal life means knowing ... It means knowing
decisions.reason: Readable uses "knowing" to show that the knowing goes on (meaning decision m2), and says it twice so the reader sees that the Son is known together with the Father (meaning decision m3).

records.source: ἐγώ σε ἐδόξασα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, τὸ ἔργον τελειώσας ὃ δέδωκάς μοι ἵνα ποιήσω·
records.gloss: I you glorified on the earth, the work having completed that you have given me that I should do.

L.4: I glorified {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} on the earth, having completed the work which {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} to do.

R.4: I have brought glory to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} here on earth. I have finished the work {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} to do.

decisions.choice: Jesus glorified the Father by doing the work the Father gave him
decisions.reason: Jesus's whole life has shown who the Father is: his signs revealed God's glory (2:11; 11:4, 40), and his words were the Father's (12:49-50). He has said from the start that his food is to do the will of the one who sent him and to finish his work (4:34), and that his works bear witness that the Father sent him (5:36). The "I" is emphatic: this is what the Son has done; verse 5 asks what the Father will do.

decisions.choice: having completed: the work is spoken of as done, though the cross is still ahead
alternatives: the work of teaching only, apart from the cross
decisions.reason: τελειώσας is an aorist participle: the Son has brought the work to its goal. As in 13:31, Jesus speaks from the hour itself, so the cross that completes the work is counted with it. "On earth" sets this beside verse 5, where he asks for glory in the Father's presence.

decisions.choice: a link with Jesus's last word on the cross, "It is finished" (19:30)
decisions.reason: On the cross Jesus says Τετέλεσται (19:30), a closely related verb, and John uses this verb for the completing of Scripture just before (19:28). The work he says here is complete is the one he declares finished there. John does not mark the link, so it is noted as likely, not certain.

decisions.choice: have glorified ... by completing (B); have brought glory to ... I have finished (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced shows by "by" how the Father was glorified (meaning decision m1). Readable says "brought glory to" as elsewhere in the prayer and makes the two parts two sentences.

records.source: καὶ νῦν δόξασόν με σύ, πάτερ, παρὰ σεαυτῷ τῇ δόξῃ ᾗ εἶχον πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι παρὰ σοί.
records.gloss: And now glorify me you, Father, with yourself with the glory which I was having before the the world to be with you.

L.5: And now, Father, glorify {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} with {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}, with the glory which I had with {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} before the world existed.

R.5: So now, Father, bring glory to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} at {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} side. Give {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} the glory I had with {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} before the world began.

decisions.choice: glorify me with yourself: in the Father's own presence, by the Father himself
alternatives: in your sight, in your judgment
decisions.reason: "And now" turns from what the Son has done on earth (verse 4) to what he asks the Father to do. The "you" is emphatic: the Father himself is to glorify him. "With yourself" means beside the Father, in his presence, set against "on earth" in verse 4. Jesus is asking to return to where he came from (13:3; 16:28).

decisions.choice: the glory I had with you before the world existed: the Son shared the Father's glory before creation
alternatives: the glory planned for him before the world, not yet his
decisions.reason: The Son speaks of a glory he had with the Father before the world existed, which fits what John says at the start: in the beginning the Word was with God and was God (1:1-2), and all things came into being through him (1:3). The imperfect "I had" describes a lasting state. In Isaiah God says that he gives his glory to no other (Isaiah 42:8), yet the Son had this glory with him. The verse asks for that glory now, in the Father's presence; it does not say that the Son ever stopped being who he was. Compare 17:24.

decisions.choice: the world: the created order
decisions.reason: Here the world is the whole creation, as in 1:10a and 17:24: the glory was there before anything was made.

decisions.choice: yourself, at your side, was mine (B); at your side, Give me the glory I had (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced shows the emphatic "you" with "yourself" and says "at your side" for the Father's presence (meaning decision m1). Readable splits the request and says "before the world began", plainer than "existed"; Balanced says "before there was a world".

records.source: Ἐφανέρωσά σου τὸ ὄνομα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις οὓς ἔδωκάς μοι ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου.
records.gloss: I made manifest of you the name to the men whom you gave me out of the world.

L.6: I revealed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name to the {{gender:people|men}} whom {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} out of the world.

R.6: I have shown who {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are to the {{gender:people|men}} {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} from the world.

decisions.choice: your name: the Father himself, as he has made himself known
alternatives: a particular new name for God
decisions.reason: In the Bible a name stands for the person as he has shown himself to be. God made his name known to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14-15) and proclaimed it on the mountain, as the God who is merciful and gracious, rich in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exodus 34:5-7). Jesus has made the Father known in the same way: whoever has seen him has seen the Father (1:18; 14:9). Compare 12:28 and 17:26.

decisions.choice: revealed: made visible, brought into the open
decisions.reason: Ἐφανέρωσά means to make visible what was hidden. John uses it of Jesus being revealed to Israel (1:31) and of his glory shown in his signs (2:11). The Father has been shown in what Jesus has said and done.

decisions.choice: whom you gave me out of the world: the disciples, given by the Father and taken from the world
decisions.reason: The people meant are first of all the disciples with Jesus that night. They are the Father's gift to him (6:37, 39; 10:29), and they are taken "out of" the world, the mass of humanity that does not know God (15:19; 17:14-16), while they still live in it (17:11, 15).

decisions.choice: the people: human beings, not men in contrast with women
decisions.reason: The word means human beings. Though the disciples at the table are men, the gift of the Father is spoken of in general terms, and the prayer reaches out to all who will believe (17:20).

decisions.choice: {{gender:people|men}}
decisions.reason: The inclusive "people" is the default and "men" the alternative (meaning decision m4), as at 1:4 and 3:19.

decisions.choice: shown who you are
decisions.reason: Readable says what making the Father's name known means (meaning decision m1), since "your name" alone may sound like only a word.

records.heading: Jesus prays for his disciples

records.source: σοὶ ἦσαν κἀμοὶ αὐτοὺς ἔδωκας, καὶ τὸν λόγον σου τετήρηκαν.
records.gloss: To you they were, and to me them you gave, and the word of you they have kept.

L.6: They were {{deity_pronoun:yours|Yours}}, and to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave them, and they have kept {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} word.

R.6: They were {{deity_pronoun:yours|Yours}}, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave them to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. And they have obeyed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} word.

decisions.choice: they were yours, and you gave them to me: they belonged to the Father before they came to Jesus
decisions.reason: The disciples did not first belong to Jesus and then to God; they were the Father's, and he gave them to the Son (6:37, 44, 65; 10:29). "To me" is emphatic, joined to "and" in one word. The text says that they were the Father's but not how; it does not explain it further.

decisions.choice: kept: held fast to and obeyed
decisions.reason: To keep a word is to hold on to it and do what it says (8:51; 14:23; 15:20). The perfect tense says they have kept it and still do. The disciples will fail Jesus that very night (16:32), but Jesus speaks of their faith as a whole.

decisions.choice: your word: the Father's message, which Jesus spoke
decisions.reason: The word the disciples kept is the Father's, given through Jesus: the word they hear from Jesus is not his own but the Father's who sent him (14:24). Verse 8 speaks of the same thing in the plural, "the words".

decisions.choice: belonged to you (B); obeyed (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says "belonged to" for the plain "were yours". Readable says "obeyed", the everyday sense of keeping a word (meaning decision m2), so that "kept your word" is not read as keeping a promise.

records.source: νῦν ἔγνωκαν ὅτι πάντα ὅσα δέδωκάς μοι παρὰ σοῦ εἰσιν·
records.gloss: Now they have known that all things as many as you have given me from you are.

L.7: Now they have known that all things whatever {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} are from {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.

R.7: Now they understand that all the things {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} came from {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.

decisions.choice: they have known (SBLGNT)
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts read "they have known". A few read "I have known", and a few have other forms of the verb. "They" fits the flow of the prayer, which in verses 6-8 is all about what the disciples have received and believed. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: now they have come to know: a knowing reached and still held
decisions.reason: ἔγνωκαν is perfect tense: they have come to know and now know. "Now" looks back to the last words of the disciples at the supper: "Now we know ... we believe that you came from God" (16:30).

decisions.choice: all you have given me: everything Jesus has, his words and his works, comes from the Father
decisions.reason: What the disciples have come to see is that nothing in Jesus is his own apart from the Father: his words (verse 8; 12:49), his works (5:36), and his authority (17:2). That is the knowing that leads to the faith of verse 8.

decisions.choice: have come to know (B); understand (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced shows the perfect tense, knowing reached and still held (meaning decision m2). Readable says "understand", the everyday word for knowing of this kind.

records.source: ὅτι τὰ ῥήματα ἃ ἔδωκάς μοι δέδωκα αὐτοῖς, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἔλαβον καὶ ἔγνωσαν ἀληθῶς ὅτι παρὰ σοῦ ἐξῆλθον, καὶ ἐπίστευσαν ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας.
records.gloss: Because the words which you gave me I have given to them, and they received and knew truly that from you I came out, and they believed that you me sent.

L.8: For the words which {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} I have given to them, and they received [them] and knew truly that from {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} I came out, and they believed that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.8: This is because I gave them the words {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and they accepted them. They know for sure that I came from {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, and they believe that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: for: this explains how the disciples came to know (verse 7)
decisions.reason: ὅτι here gives the reason for verse 7: they know that everything Jesus has comes from the Father because he gave them the Father's words, and they received them.

decisions.choice: the words: the sayings Jesus spoke, all of which came from the Father
decisions.reason: The plural ῥήματα means the things Jesus said one by one; the singular "word" in verse 6 is the message as a whole. Jesus has said that he speaks only what the Father told him (12:49-50; 14:10). John uses the plural for the words that give life (6:63, 68).

decisions.choice: knew truly: came to know with real certainty
decisions.reason: ἀληθῶς means "truly" or "in truth": their knowing is real and sure. The aorist tenses (received, knew, believed) speak of what happened when they took in Jesus's words.

decisions.choice: I came from you ... you sent me: Jesus's origin with the Father and his mission from him
decisions.reason: Two ways of saying the same truth: Jesus came out from the Father, and the Father sent him. The disciples said just this at 16:30 ("we believe that you came from God"), and Jesus answered it at 16:27-28. The "you" in "you sent me" is emphatic: it was the Father, and no other, who sent him. Believing that the Father sent him is what the Gospel asks of everyone (11:42; 17:21; 20:31).

decisions.choice: For I have passed on to them ... it was you who sent me (B); This is because ... you are the one who sent me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the verb first and breaks the long sentence in two. Literal brackets [them], which the Greek leaves understood after "received"; the other levels supply it. Readable says "This is because" to tie the sentence to verse 7 (meaning decision m1) and uses the present "know" and "believe" for knowing and faith that last. Balanced and Readable show the emphatic "you" (meaning decision m4), as 11:42 does.

records.source: ἐγὼ περὶ αὐτῶν ἐρωτῶ· οὐ περὶ τοῦ κόσμου ἐρωτῶ ἀλλὰ περὶ ὧν δέδωκάς μοι, ὅτι σοί εἰσιν, καὶ τὰ ἐμὰ πάντα σά ἐστιν καὶ τὰ σὰ ἐμά, καὶ δεδόξασμαι ἐν αὐτοῖς.
records.gloss: I concerning them ask; not concerning the world I ask but concerning [those] whom you have given me, because yours they are, \v 10 and the mine all yours is and the yours mine, and I have been glorified in them.

L.9: I am asking concerning them; I am not asking concerning the world, but concerning those whom {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, because they are {{deity_pronoun:yours|Yours}},
L.10: and all things that are {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}} are {{deity_pronoun:yours|Yours}}, and {{deity_pronoun:yours|Yours}} [are] {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}}, and I have been glorified in them.

R.9: I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world, but for the people {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, because they belong to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.
R.10: Everything that is {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}} is {{deity_pronoun:yours|Yours}}, and everything that is {{deity_pronoun:yours|Yours}} is {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}}. And {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} glory has been shown in them.

decisions.choice: I am asking: Jesus makes a request of the Father on behalf of the disciples
decisions.reason: The verb ἐρωτῶ can mean to ask a question or to make a request. In the farewell discourses John uses it for Jesus's requests to the Father (14:16; 16:26), and it runs through this prayer (17:15, 20). The pronoun "I" is stated, which gives weight to it: Jesus himself intercedes for them.

decisions.choice: not for the world: in this part of the prayer Jesus prays for his disciples; it does not mean that the world is outside God's love
alternatives: Jesus refuses to pray for the world at all
decisions.reason: God loved the world and sent the Son to save it (3:16-17), and later in this same prayer Jesus asks that the world may believe and know that the Father sent him (17:21, 23). Here the request is narrower: it is for the people the Father has given him, who are about to be left in a hostile world (17:11, 14). The sentence says who this request is for, not who God cares about.

decisions.choice: all things that are mine are yours: a complete sharing of everything between the Son and the Father, of which the disciples are a part
alternatives: all the people who are mine are yours
decisions.reason: The words for "mine" and "yours" are neuter plural, "all things", not just "all the people". Jesus has said the same in 16:15 ("all that the Father has is mine"). The disciples are included in that sharing: they were the Father's, he gave them to the Son (17:6), and they remain the Father's.

decisions.choice: I have been glorified in them: Jesus's glory has already been shown in the disciples, who received his words and believed
alternatives: I will be glorified in them, spoken of the future as already done
decisions.reason: The verb δεδόξασμαι is perfect: something done that still stands. In 17:6-8 Jesus has said that the disciples kept the Father's word, received his words and believed that the Father sent him. Their faith shows who he is, and so he is glorified in them. The coming glory of the cross (17:1, 5) is still ahead, so some read the perfect as looking forward; the context points to what has already happened.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}}, {{deity_pronoun:yours|Yours}}, {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}} for the Father; {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}}, {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} for Jesus; {{deity_pronoun:we|We}} for the Father and the Son
decisions.reason: The whole passage is Jesus's prayer to the Father. Every pronoun for the Father ("you", "your", "yours", "yourself") and every pronoun Jesus uses of himself except "I" takes the deity_pronoun setting, as does "we" for the Father and the Son together (as 14:23). At the start of a sentence the pronoun is written plain.

decisions.choice: asking (L, B); praying (R); my glory has been shown in them (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "ask", so the repeated verb stays visible here and in 17:15 and 17:20. Readable says "praying", the everyday word for asking God for something (meaning decision m1). Readable turns the passive "I have been glorified in them" around so that it is easy to follow, and keeps "glory" (meaning decision m4).

records.source: καὶ οὐκέτι εἰμὶ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ εἰσίν, κἀγὼ πρὸς σὲ ἔρχομαι.
records.gloss: And no longer I am in the world, and they in the world are, and I to you am coming.

L.11: And I am no longer in the world, and they are in the world, and I am coming to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.

R.11: Soon I will not be in the world any longer, but they will still be in the world. I am coming to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}.

decisions.choice: I am no longer in the world: Jesus speaks of his departure as though it has already happened
alternatives: Jesus has already left the world
decisions.reason: Jesus is still with the disciples and still speaking "in the world" (17:13), but his hour has come (17:1) and he is on his way to the Father (13:1; 16:28). The present tense looks at his going as settled. "I am coming to you" says the same thing from the other side.

decisions.choice: and they are in the world: a contrast; the disciples stay behind in the world that Jesus is leaving
decisions.reason: The pronoun αὐτοὶ ("they") is stated, setting the disciples against Jesus: he is going, they are staying. The world here is the world of people that hates them (17:14), which is why they need the Father's keeping in the next sentence.

decisions.choice: but ... still (B); Soon I will no longer be ... will still be (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "but" for the "and" of contrast and add "still" (meaning decision m2). Readable adds "Soon" and "any longer" and uses the future so that a young reader is not puzzled that Jesus, who is speaking, says he is no longer in the world (meaning decision m1).

records.source: πάτερ ἅγιε, τήρησον αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί σου ᾧ δέδωκάς μοι, ἵνα ὦσιν ἓν καθὼς ἡμεῖς.
records.gloss: Father holy, keep them in the name of you which you have given me, so that they may be one just as we.

L.11: Holy Father, keep them in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name, which {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, so that they may be one just as {{deity_pronoun:we|We}} [are].

R.11: Holy Father, keep them safe by the power of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name, the name {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. Then they will be one, just as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} and I are one.

decisions.choice: which you have given me: the Father has given his name to the Son (ᾧ, agreeing with "name")
alternatives: whom you have given me: the Father has given the disciples to the Son (οὓς)
that which you have given me (a neuter relative)
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads ᾧ, the relative pronoun in the case of "name": the name is what the Father gave. This is the reading of most early manuscripts. Some manuscripts, mainly later ones and some of the Western tradition, read οὓς ("those whom"), making the disciples what was given, and a few have a neuter relative. Copyists were more likely to change the unusual idea of a name given to the Son into the familiar idea of disciples given to him (17:6, 9) than the reverse. The same variation appears in 17:12. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Holy Father: a unique address that stresses the Father's holiness, and ties this request to "sanctify" in 17:17 and 17:19
decisions.reason: Nowhere else in the New Testament is God addressed as "Holy Father"; later Jesus says "righteous Father" (17:25). ἅγιε ("holy") shares its root with the verb "sanctify" (make holy) in 17:17 and 17:19: the holy Father is asked to keep the disciples and to make them his own.

decisions.choice: keep them in your name: guard them by the power of the Father's name, as people who belong to it
alternatives: keep them faithful to your name
decisions.reason: In the Bible God's name stands for God himself as he has made himself known, with his power and authority (Psalm 20:2; Proverbs 18:10). Jesus has made that name known to the disciples (17:6). "In" carries both ideas: by the protecting power of the name, and within the circle of those who bear it. The name was given to the Son (compare Exodus 23:21, "my name is in him"; Philippians 2:9), so Jesus has been keeping them in it (17:12).

decisions.choice: so that they may be one just as we are: the unity of the disciples is modeled on the unity of the Father and the Son
decisions.reason: "We" is the Father and the Son, whose oneness Jesus has spoken of before (10:30). The disciples' unity is meant to reflect it, and the prayer returns to this at length in 17:21-23.

decisions.choice: just as {{deity_pronoun:we|We}} [are] (L); just as {{deity_pronoun:we|We}} are one (B); just as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} and I are one (R)
decisions.reason: "We" means the Father and the Son, so it takes the deity_pronoun setting, as in 14:23. Readable names the two ("you and I"), which avoids an unclear "we"; "you" takes the setting and "I" does not. Balanced and Readable repeat "one" where the Greek leaves it understood.

decisions.choice: the name you have given me (B, R); keep them safe by the power of your name (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable repeat "the name" so that it is clear that the name is what was given (meaning decision m1). Readable spells out what "in your name" means (meaning decision m3) and starts a new sentence with "Then" for the purpose clause.

records.source: ὅτε ἤμην μετ’ αὐτῶν ἐγὼ ἐτήρουν αὐτοὺς ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί σου ᾧ δέδωκάς μοι, καὶ ἐφύλαξα, καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀπώλετο εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας, ἵνα ἡ γραφὴ πληρωθῇ.
records.gloss: When I was with them, I was keeping them in the name of you which you have given me, and I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of the destruction, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

L.12: When I was with them, I was keeping them in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name, which {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and I guarded [them], and not one of them perished except the son of perishing, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled.

R.12: While I was with them, I kept them safe by the power of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name, the name {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. I guarded them, and not one of them was lost except the one who was doomed to be lost. This happened so that what the Scripture says would come true.

decisions.choice: the son of destruction: the one marked out for destruction, the one doomed to be lost; Judas
decisions.reason: "Son of" with a noun is a Hebrew way of saying what a person belongs to or is headed for (compare "sons of disobedience", Ephesians 2:2). The noun ἀπωλείας comes from the same root as the verb ἀπώλετο just before it, "perished" or "was lost": none was lost except the one belonging to lostness. The words name Judas, whom Jesus already knew would hand him over (6:70-71; 13:18, 21-27). The same title is used for the man of lawlessness in 2 Thessalonians 2:3.

decisions.choice: the Scripture: most likely Psalm 41:10, already quoted of Judas in 13:18
alternatives: Psalm 109:8, applied to Judas in Acts 1:20
Scripture in general, without one verse in view
decisions.reason: John does not say which passage he means. In 13:18 Jesus quoted Psalm 41 ("the one who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me") of Judas, and said it was spoken "so that the Scripture may be fulfilled", the same phrase as here. Acts 1:20 applies Psalm 69 and Psalm 109 to Judas. Since only the general phrase is given, the reference is uncertain.

decisions.choice: Judas's loss was not a failure of Jesus's keeping: the Scripture had foretold it
decisions.reason: The imperfect ἐτήρουν ("I was keeping") describes Jesus's steady care through his ministry, and the aorist ἐφύλαξα ("I guarded") sums it up. Jesus said he would lose none of those the Father gave him (6:39; 10:28), and he repeats it in 18:9. Judas is named as the exception, but not as one the Father had given and the Son failed to keep: his path was foretold in Scripture, and he chose it (13:2, 27).

decisions.choice: in your name, which you have given me: as in 17:11, the name is what was given
alternatives: those whom you have given me I guarded
decisions.reason: As in 17:11, the SBLGNT reads ᾧ, referring to the name. Many later manuscripts read οὓς here and join it to the next verb: "I kept them in your name; those whom you gave me I guarded." The early manuscripts support the reading followed here. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: perished ... the son of perishing (L); was lost ... the one doomed to be lost (B, R)
alternatives: was lost ... the son of destruction
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the wordplay between the verb and the noun (meaning decision m1). Literal uses "perish" for both, as it does for the same verb in 3:16 and 10:28, and keeps the Hebrew shape "son of". Balanced and Readable explain the idiom and use "lost", which suits the picture of a shepherd guarding his sheep (10:28; 18:9). "Son of perdition" is the familiar older wording.

records.source: νῦν δὲ πρὸς σὲ ἔρχομαι, καὶ ταῦτα λαλῶ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἵνα ἔχωσιν τὴν χαρὰν τὴν ἐμὴν πεπληρωμένην ἐν ἑαυτοῖς.
records.gloss: But now to you I am coming, and these things I speak in the world so that they may have the joy the mine having been made full in themselves.

L.13: But now I am coming to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, and these things I speak in the world so that they may have the joy that is {{deity_pronoun:mine|Mine}} made full in themselves.

R.13: Now I am coming to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}. I am saying all this while I am still in the world, so that they will be full of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} joy.

decisions.choice: these things I speak in the world: Jesus prays aloud, in the disciples' hearing, while he is still in the world
decisions.reason: "These things" are the words of this prayer, and perhaps the whole farewell discourse. Jesus speaks them where the disciples can hear (compare 11:42, where he prays aloud for the sake of the crowd), so that they will know what he has asked for them. "In the world" stands against "I am coming to you": he is still here, but not for long (17:11).

decisions.choice: my joy made full in them: the joy Jesus has in his union with the Father, given to the disciples and completed in them
decisions.reason: This is the promise of 15:11 and 16:20-24 again. The joy is Jesus's own, the joy of the Son who obeys and is loved by the Father (15:10-11). The perfect participle πεπληρωμένην ("having been made full") describes a joy filled and staying full, as in 16:24.

decisions.choice: made full (L); complete (B); full (R); while still (B), while I am still (R)
decisions.reason: The same wording as 15:11 and 16:24 at each level, since this is the same promise. "Joy" is the key term at every level. Balanced and Readable add "while still" to bring out the contrast with "I am coming to you" (meaning decision m1).

records.source: ἐγὼ δέδωκα αὐτοῖς τὸν λόγον σου, καὶ ὁ κόσμος ἐμίσησεν αὐτούς, ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου καθὼς ἐγὼ οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου.
records.gloss: I have given them the word of you, and the world hated them, because not they are of the world just as I not am of the world.

L.14: I have given them {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} word, and the world hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.

R.14: I have given {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} word to them, and the world has come to hate them. That is because they do not belong to the world, just as I do not belong to the world.

decisions.choice: your word: the Father's message as a whole, which Jesus has passed on to the disciples
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks only what the Father gave him (12:49-50; 17:8, "the words you gave me"). The disciples have kept that word (17:6), and it is this word that sets them apart from the world (17:17).

decisions.choice: the world hated them: the world's hatred is already a fact
decisions.reason: The verb ἐμίσησεν is aorist, stating it as something that has happened. Jesus has already warned them of it (15:18-21; 16:2-3), and the hatred that is about to fall on him includes them. The world here is humanity organized against God (15:18).

decisions.choice: not of the world: not belonging to the world, not having their origin and character from it
decisions.reason: "Of" means origin and belonging, as in 15:19 and 8:23 ("you are of this world; I am not of this world"). The disciples still live in the world (17:11, 15), but they take their life from the Father, as Jesus does.

decisions.choice: do not belong to the world (B, R); has hated / has come to hate (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Belong to" says plainly what "of" means here (meaning decision m3), as 15:19 does. The English perfect "has hated" fits a hatred that has begun and goes on (meaning decision m2).

records.source: οὐκ ἐρωτῶ ἵνα ἄρῃς αὐτοὺς ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου ἀλλ’ ἵνα τηρήσῃς αὐτοὺς ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ.
records.gloss: Not I ask that you take them out of the world but that you keep them from the evil [one].

L.15: I do not ask that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} take them out of the world, but that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} keep them from the evil [one].

R.15: I am not asking {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} to take them out of the world. I am asking {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} to keep them safe from the evil one.

decisions.choice: the evil one: the devil
decisions.reason: The form πονηροῦ can be masculine ("the evil one") or neuter ("evil"). John's writings use "the evil one" for the devil (1 John 2:13-14; 3:12; 5:18-19, "the evil one does not touch him ... the whole world lies in the evil one"), and Jesus has spoken of "the ruler of the world" (12:31; 14:30; 16:11). The same question arises in Matthew 6:13. A general prayer for protection from evil is also possible, so the choice is not certain.

decisions.choice: not taken out of the world, but kept from the evil one: the disciples stay in the world but are guarded out of the evil one's reach
decisions.reason: Jesus does not ask for escape. The disciples are sent into the world (17:18) and must stay there. The verb τηρήσῃς ("keep") is the one used in 17:11-12: the Father is to go on doing what Jesus did while he was with them.

decisions.choice: keep them safe from (B, R); the evil [one] (L)
decisions.reason: "Keep ... safe" makes clear that keeping here means protecting, as in 17:11-12. Literal brackets "one", which Greek leaves understood with the adjective.

records.source: ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου οὐκ εἰσὶν καθὼς ἐγὼ οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου.
records.gloss: Of the world not they are just as I not am of the world.

L.16: Of the world they are not, just as I am not of the world.

R.16: They do not belong to the world, just as I do not.

decisions.choice: they are not of the world: a repetition of 17:14 that stresses the point and leads into the request of 17:17
decisions.reason: The sentence repeats 17:14 almost word for word, but now "of the world" comes first, giving it weight. The world's hatred has been mentioned; now Jesus restates why it happens, and why the disciples need to be set apart by the truth (17:17).

decisions.choice: of the world: belonging to the world and taking one's life from it
decisions.reason: As in 17:14 and 15:19, "of" means origin and belonging (8:23).

decisions.choice: Of the world they are not (L)
alternatives: They are not of the world (L)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek order, which puts "of the world" first for emphasis (meaning decision m1). Balanced and Readable use the same wording as 17:14.

records.source: ἁγίασον αὐτοὺς ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ· ὁ λόγος ὁ σὸς ἀλήθειά ἐστιν.
records.gloss: Sanctify them in the truth; the word the yours truth is.

L.17: Sanctify them in the truth; {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} word is truth.

R.17: Set them apart for {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} and make them holy by the truth. Your word is truth.

decisions.choice: sanctify: set them apart for God, make them holy and his own, for his service
decisions.reason: The verb ἁγίασον means to make holy, that is, to set apart as belonging to God. In the Old Testament it is used of priests consecrated for service (Exodus 28:41; 29:1) and of what is set apart for God (Exodus 13:2). John used it of Jesus himself, "whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world" (10:36). Moral purity follows from belonging to God, but the main idea is being his and set apart for his purpose, here the mission of 17:18. The verb shares its root with "Holy Father" (17:11).

decisions.choice: in the truth: by means of the truth, and so into the truth
alternatives: in the sphere of the truth only
decisions.reason: The preposition can mean "in" or "by". The next words, "your word is truth", explain it: the Father's word, which Jesus has given them (17:14), is what sets them apart. To be set apart by the truth is also to live in it.

decisions.choice: your word is truth: probably an echo of Psalm 119:142 ("your law is truth")
decisions.reason: The wording is close to Psalm 119:142 and 119:160 ("the sum of your word is truth"). In John the truth is God's reality made known, and Jesus himself is the truth (14:6). Whether the psalm is in view or the saying simply sums up the Father's word is uncertain.

decisions.choice: sanctify (L); set apart (B); set apart ... and make holy (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "sanctify", the traditional word, and uses it again in 17:19 so the link is plain. Balanced says "set apart", as in 10:36, and uses it again in 17:19. Readable uses "set apart" and adds "make holy" so that both sides of the word are clear (meaning decision m1). "Truth" is the key term at every level.

decisions.choice: for {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}} (B); for {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say for whom they are set apart: for God, whose holiness they share (meaning decision m1). "Set apart" on its own could leave this unclear.

records.source: καθὼς ἐμὲ ἀπέστειλας εἰς τὸν κόσμον, κἀγὼ ἀπέστειλα αὐτοὺς εἰς τὸν κόσμον·
records.gloss: Just as me you sent into the world, I also sent them into the world;

L.18: Just as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} into the world, I also sent them into the world.

R.18: You sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} into the world. In the same way, I have sent them into the world.

decisions.choice: the disciples' mission is patterned on Jesus's own: as the Father sent him, so he sends them
decisions.reason: Jesus is "the one sent" throughout John (3:17; 5:36; 17:3, 8). Now his disciples share his mission (13:20; 20:21, "as the Father has sent me, I also send you"). This is why Jesus does not ask that they be taken out of the world (17:15).

decisions.choice: I sent them: the sending is spoken of as already done
decisions.reason: The verb ἀπέστειλα is aorist. Jesus has already sent them out once (4:38, "I sent you to reap"), and their commission is complete in his mind, though it is given in full after the resurrection (20:21).

decisions.choice: I in the same way have sent (B); In the same way, I have sent (R)
decisions.reason: "In the same way" brings out the matching of the two sendings (meaning decision m1), and the English perfect suits a sending that stands (meaning decision m2).

records.source: καὶ ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἐγὼ ἁγιάζω ἐμαυτόν, ἵνα ὦσιν καὶ αὐτοὶ ἡγιασμένοι ἐν ἀληθείᾳ.
records.gloss: And for them I sanctify myself, so that may be also they having been sanctified in truth.

L.19: And for their sake I sanctify {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, so that they also may be sanctified in truth.

R.19: For their sake I set {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} apart for {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, so that they too may be set apart and made holy by the truth.

decisions.choice: I sanctify myself: Jesus dedicates himself to God for his death, offered on their behalf
alternatives: Jesus dedicates himself to his mission in general
decisions.reason: The verb ἁγιάζω is the one used for setting apart priests and sacrifices for God (Exodus 28:41; Deuteronomy 15:19). "For their sake" uses ὑπὲρ, the preposition John uses for Jesus's death on behalf of others (10:11, 15; 11:50-52; 15:13). Spoken on the night before the cross, the words most likely mean that he gives himself to God as an offering. They could also mean his dedication to the whole work the Father gave him (10:36; 17:4); the text does not say more.

decisions.choice: so that they may be sanctified in truth: their being set apart depends on his, and lasts
decisions.reason: The perfect participle ἡγιασμένοι ("having been sanctified") describes a lasting state. The disciples are set apart because Jesus has set himself apart for them: what he asked the Father to do in 17:17 rests on what he does here. The same verb, used three times in 17:17-19, links his self-giving and their consecration.

decisions.choice: in truth: in the truth of 17:17, not merely "truly"
decisions.reason: Here "truth" has no article, and the phrase could mean "truly", as it sometimes does. Coming just after "sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth" (17:17), it most likely picks up the same truth. Either way the sense is close.

decisions.choice: sanctify ... sanctified (L); set apart ... set apart (B, R); for you, made holy (R)
decisions.reason: Each level uses the same verb as it did in 17:17, so that the link between Jesus's self-giving and the disciples' consecration is visible (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable say "by the truth" as in 17:17 (meaning decision m3). Readable adds "for you" and "made holy", as in 17:17. "Truth" is the key term at every level.

records.source: Οὐ περὶ τούτων δὲ ἐρωτῶ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τῶν πιστευόντων διὰ τοῦ λόγου αὐτῶν εἰς ἐμέ, ἵνα πάντες ἓν ὦσιν, καθὼς σύ, πάτερ, ἐν ἐμοὶ κἀγὼ ἐν σοί, ἵνα καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἡμῖν ὦσιν, ἵνα ὁ κόσμος πιστεύῃ ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας.
records.gloss: Not concerning these but I ask only, but also concerning the [ones] believing through the word of them into me, \v 21 that all one may be, just as you, Father, in me and I in you, that also they in us may be, that the world may believe that you me sent.
pieces: those who are going to believe

L.20: And I am not asking on behalf of these only, but also on behalf of those who believe in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} through their word,
L.21: that all may be one, just as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, Father, [are] in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and I in {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, that they also may be in {{deity_pronoun:us|Us}}, so that the world may believe that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.20: I am not praying only for these disciples. I am also praying for all who will believe in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} because of their message.
R.21: Father, I pray that all of them will be one, just as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and I am in {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}. I pray that they will be in {{deity_pronoun:us|Us}} too. Then the world will believe that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: those who believe in me through their word: the people who will come to believe through the disciples' message
alternatives: only those who already believed at the time
decisions.reason: The participle πιστευόντων is present, "the believing ones", but it is defined by "through their word": the word of the disciples Jesus has just been praying for (17:6-19), whom he is sending into the world (17:18). So Jesus's prayer reaches beyond the Eleven to all who will believe through their witness (compare 20:29, 31). "Their word" is the disciples' message about Jesus, which is his own word passed on (17:8, 14).

decisions.choice: one: neuter, "one thing", a unity of many persons, not one person
decisions.reason: "All" (πάντες) is masculine plural, but "one" (ἓν) is neuter, as when Jesus says "I and the Father are one" (10:30). The many believers do not become one person or lose who they are; they are made one, as the Father and the Son are two and yet one (17:11, 22).

decisions.choice: the unity is modelled on, and drawn from, the unity of the Father and the Son: believers are one by being in the Father and the Son
alternatives: agreement of opinion or purpose only
a hidden, inward unity that the world cannot see
decisions.reason: The pattern is "just as you, Father, are in me and I in you": the Father and the Son live in each other. Jesus then asks that believers "also may be in us", so their oneness with each other comes from their sharing in that life (14:20; 15:4-5). It is not mere agreement, and it is not only invisible either: it is to be seen, so that the world may believe (compare 13:34-35, where the world knows his disciples by their love for one another). The passage does not say what outward form this unity takes.

decisions.choice: the first two "that" clauses say what Jesus asks; the third gives the purpose of it all, that the world may believe
alternatives: each "that" clause depends on the one before it, a chain of purposes
the second "that" clause gives the purpose of the "just as" clause
decisions.reason: The sentence has three clauses with ἵνα. The first two say much the same thing and are best read as the content of Jesus's request: that all may be one, and, put more fully, that they may be in the Father and the Son. The third states what the request is for: that the world may believe. The same shape returns in 17:22-23. The word can introduce either the content of a request or its purpose, so the links between the clauses are not certain; the meaning of the whole is not much affected.

decisions.choice: that they also may be in us, as the SBLGNT reads
alternatives: that they also may be one in us (Codex Sinaiticus and most later manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "one" here, "that they also may be one in us", which repeats the "one" of the clause before. Some important early manuscripts, among them Codex Vaticanus, do not have it, and the SBLGNT follows them. The addition is easy to explain as a copyist making the two clauses match. The sense is close either way. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity that does not yet believe, which may still come to believe
alternatives: humanity set against God, with no hope of believing
decisions.reason: In this prayer "the world" is often the human world that hates Jesus and his disciples (17:14, 25). Here, as in 3:16-17, it is the same world seen as the object of God's mission: the unity of believers is meant to lead it to believe that the Father sent the Son.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}}, {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:we|We}}, {{deity_pronoun:us|Us}}
decisions.reason: John 17 is a prayer to the Father, so every "you" and "your" spoken to him uses the deity_pronoun setting, as do "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself, and "we" and "us" for the Father and the Son together (as in 14:23). "I" takes no span. This applies throughout the passage. "They", "them" and "all" are plural and need no gender setting.

decisions.choice: asking on behalf of (L, B); praying for (R); who are going to believe (B), who will believe (R); word (L), message (B, R)
decisions.reason: The verb means "ask", and with this preposition "ask on behalf of"; "asking for these" would sound as if Jesus were asking to be given them. Readable says "praying", which is what the asking is. Balanced and Readable say "are going to believe" and "will believe", since those meant are people who will come to believe later (meaning decision m1), and "message" for the disciples' "word", so that it is not taken as a single word.

decisions.choice: My prayer is also for, I ask that, so may they (B); these disciples, I pray that, Then (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable break the long sentence and repeat that Jesus is asking or praying, so that each "that" clause is plainly part of his request (meaning decision m4). Readable names "these disciples" and says "Then" for the clause of purpose. Both move "Father" to the start of the request, where English puts an address.

records.heading: Jesus prays for all who will believe

records.source: κἀγὼ τὴν δόξαν ἣν δέδωκάς μοι δέδωκα αὐτοῖς, ἵνα ὦσιν ἓν καθὼς ἡμεῖς ἕν, ἐγὼ ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ σὺ ἐν ἐμοί, ἵνα ὦσιν τετελειωμένοι εἰς ἕν, ἵνα γινώσκῃ ὁ κόσμος ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας καὶ ἠγάπησας αὐτοὺς καθὼς ἐμὲ ἠγάπησας.
records.gloss: And I the glory which you have given to me have given to them, that they may be one just as we one, \v 23 I in them and you in me, that they may be having been perfected into one, that may know the world that you me sent and loved them just as me you loved.

L.22: And the glory that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} I have given to them, so that they may be one just as {{deity_pronoun:we|We}} [are] one,
L.23: I in them and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, so that they may be perfected into one, so that the world may know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and loved them just as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} loved {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.22: I have given them the glory that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} gave {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, so that they may be one, just as {{deity_pronoun:we|We}} are one.
R.23: I am in them, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are in {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. May they be made completely one. Then the world will know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. It will know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} love them just as {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} love {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: the glory: the Father's own presence and life shown in the Son, which the Son shares with his own and which makes them one
alternatives: the glory of the age to come, still to be given
the honor of suffering and dying as Jesus does
decisions.reason: John does not say what this glory is, and the reading is uncertain. In this Gospel glory is God himself made known: the Word made his home among us and "we saw his glory" (1:14), and Jesus showed it in his signs (2:11). The Father gave it to the Son (17:5, 24), and the Son has given it to his disciples in what he has made known to them (17:6-8), so that they share his life with the Father; this is why it leads to their being one. The perfect "have given" speaks of something already done. Others take it as the glory they will see and share in the age to come (17:24); others connect it with the cross, where Jesus is glorified (12:23-24; 13:31), or with the Spirit, given when he is glorified (7:39).

decisions.choice: one just as we are one: the neuter "one" again, with the oneness of Father and Son as its pattern
decisions.reason: Both times "one" (ἓν, ἕν) is neuter, as in 17:21 and 10:30, and "we" is the Father and the Son. The Greek leaves out the verb in "just as we one".

decisions.choice: I in them and you in me: says how they are to be one; the Son in them and the Father in the Son joins them to the Father
alternatives: the start of a new thought, going with what follows
decisions.reason: These words have no verb and stand between two "that" clauses. They are best read as explaining the oneness just named: the Son lives in believers and the Father in the Son, so believers are bound to the Father through the Son, and to one another (14:20; 15:4-5). They also lead into what follows, since being made one rests on this indwelling.

decisions.choice: perfected into one: brought to completion as one, a unity that reaches its full goal, by God's doing
decisions.reason: The verb τετελειωμένοι means to bring to completion or to the goal; Jesus uses it of finishing the work the Father gave him (4:34; 5:36; 17:4). It is passive, so this is something God does in them, and "into one" says what it leads to. 1 John speaks in the same way of love being made complete in those who keep God's word (1 John 2:5; 4:12).

decisions.choice: the world may know that the Father sent the Son and loves the disciples with the same love as the Son
alternatives: loved them in a lesser way than the Son
decisions.reason: As in 17:21, the world here is the human world that may still come to know (meaning decision m6 there). What it is to know is twofold: that the Father sent Jesus, and that the Father has loved the disciples "just as" he loved the Son. Jesus has said the same in 16:27 ("the Father himself loves you"). The aorist "loved" looks at the Father's love as a whole, not at one past moment.

decisions.choice: perfected into one (L); brought to perfect oneness (B); made completely one (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek "perfected into one". Balanced says "brought to perfect oneness" to keep both the idea of reaching a goal and the word "one" that runs through 17:21-23 (meaning decision m4); Readable says it plainly. The Literal "we [are] one" brackets the verb the Greek leaves out.

decisions.choice: I am in them and you are in me, So may they ... and the world will know (B); May they ..., Then the world will know ... It will know (R); you love them just as you love me (R)
alternatives: so that they may be ..., so that the world may know (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable break the long sentence and supply the verbs the Greek leaves out in "I in them and you in me" (meaning decision m3). Readable says "Then" for the clause of purpose and repeats "It will know" for the second thing the world is to know. It uses the present "love" because the Father's love for the Son and for the disciples is not over (meaning decision m5); Literal and Balanced keep "loved".

records.source: πάτερ, ὃ δέδωκάς μοι, θέλω ἵνα ὅπου εἰμὶ ἐγὼ κἀκεῖνοι ὦσιν μετ’ ἐμοῦ, ἵνα θεωρῶσιν τὴν δόξαν τὴν ἐμὴν ἣν δέδωκάς μοι, ὅτι ἠγάπησάς με πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου.
records.gloss: Father, what you have given to me, I want that where am I those also may be with me, that they may behold the glory the mine which you have given to me, because you loved me before foundation of world.

L.24: Father, what {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}: I want that where I am, they also may be with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, so that they may see {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} glory, which {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, because {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} loved {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} before [the] foundation of [the] world.

R.24: Father, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given them to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and I want them to be with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} where I am. I want them to see {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} glory. You gave {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} this glory because {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} loved {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} before the world was made.

decisions.choice: what you have given me: the believers as one whole, given by the Father to the Son; then "they" takes up each one of them
alternatives: a thing or task given to the Son
decisions.reason: The relative pronoun ὃ is neuter singular, "what", as in "all that the Father gives me will come to me" (6:37, 39) and "all that you have given him" (17:2). John speaks this way of all who belong to the Son, taken together as the Father's gift. The next words turn to the plural κἀκεῖνοι, "they too", the persons themselves.

decisions.choice: what (neuter singular), as the SBLGNT reads
alternatives: those whom (masculine plural), in many later manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "those whom", which fits the plural "they" that follows and is the easier reading. The neuter is found in important early manuscripts and matches John's way of speaking in 6:37, 39 and 17:2, so it is the more likely original; a copyist was more likely to smooth it than to create it. The sense is the same. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: I want: Jesus states his will, in full accord with the Father, not only a request
decisions.reason: Up to now Jesus has said "I ask" (17:9, 15, 20). Here he says θέλω, "I will" or "I want". The Son speaks with authority (5:21; 21:22), but not against the Father: it is the Father's will that the Son lose none of those given to him and raise them up (6:39-40). So the prayer is also a statement of what Jesus intends.

decisions.choice: to be where Jesus is and to see his glory: the glory he had with the Father before creation, given in love
alternatives: the glory seen during his life on earth
decisions.reason: "Where I am" is with the Father, where Jesus goes to prepare a place for his own (14:2-3; 12:26). There they will see his glory: the glory he had with the Father "before the world existed" (17:5), now given to him as the Son, out of a love older than the world. "The foundation of the world" means its creation. The disciples have seen his glory in part already (1:14); here they will see it fully. The verb θεωρῶσιν means to look at, to see with attention.

decisions.choice: I want (L, R); it is {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} will (B); see (all levels)
decisions.reason: Literal and Readable say "I want", the plain word. Balanced says "it is my will" so that the authority in the verb is heard (meaning decision m3); "I will" is no longer clear in modern English. "See" is used for the verb of seeing; "behold" is no longer in use.

decisions.choice: all that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} (B); {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have given them to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} (R); before the world was founded (B), made (R)
alternatives: before the foundation of the world (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the neuter "all that", which ties the verse to 6:37 and 17:2 (meaning decision m1), and then "they". Readable turns it into a plain statement about the people given to Jesus. Both say "before the world was founded" or "made" for the noun phrase, which is plainer in English. Readable repeats "I want" and "this glory" to keep its sentences short.

records.source: Πάτερ δίκαιε, καὶ ὁ κόσμος σε οὐκ ἔγνω, ἐγὼ δέ σε ἔγνων, καὶ οὗτοι ἔγνωσαν ὅτι σύ με ἀπέστειλας, καὶ ἐγνώρισα αὐτοῖς τὸ ὄνομά σου καὶ γνωρίσω, ἵνα ἡ ἀγάπη ἣν ἠγάπησάς με ἐν αὐτοῖς ᾖ κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτοῖς.
records.gloss: Father righteous, and the world you not knew, but I you knew, and these knew that you me sent; \v 26 and I made known to them the name of you and will make known, that the love [with] which you loved me in them may be, and I in them."
pieces: I will go on making it known

L.25: Righteous Father, the world indeed did not know {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, but I knew {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, and these knew that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}};
L.26: and I made known to them {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name, and I will make [it] known, so that the love with which {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} loved {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} may be in them, and I in them."

R.25: Righteous Father, the world does not know {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}. But I know {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, and these disciples know that {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.
R.26: I have made {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} name known to them. I have shown them who {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are, and I will keep on doing it. Then the love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} will be in them, and I {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} will be in them."

decisions.choice: Righteous Father: the Father who is just and does what is right, who judges between the world and those who know him
decisions.reason: Jesus calls God "righteous Father" (Πάτερ δίκαιε) only here. It fits what follows: he sets the world, which has not known the Father, against himself and the disciples, who have, and calls on the Father as the righteous judge who will rightly tell the two apart (compare 5:30; 7:24). 1 John uses the same word for God, who is righteous to forgive (1 John 1:9), and for "Jesus Christ the righteous" (1 John 2:1).

decisions.choice: the opening "and" and the "but" set the world's not knowing over against Jesus's knowing: "though the world did not know you, I knew you"
alternatives: "and" joining this sentence to the prayer before it
decisions.reason: The sentence begins with καὶ and goes on with δέ. The pairing marks a contrast: on the one side the world, on the other Jesus and these disciples. The "and" may also carry the sense "indeed" or "even". The aorists "knew" look at the whole of the world's refusal and of Jesus's knowing, not at a single moment.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity that has refused to know God
alternatives: all people, without that sense of refusal
decisions.reason: Here, unlike 17:21 and 23, the world is the human world that has turned from God: it did not know the Word through whom it was made (1:10), and it hates Jesus and his disciples because it does not know the one who sent him (15:21; 16:3). "These" are the disciples, who have known that the Father sent him (17:8).

decisions.choice: your name: the Father himself as he has made himself known; made known in Jesus's life and teaching, and to be made known still
alternatives: the name as a word or title only
decisions.reason: "Name" stands for the person and character of the Father, as in 17:6 and 17:11-12. Jesus has made the Father known in all he has said and done (1:18; 14:9). "I will make it known" looks ahead: to his death and rising, where the Father's love is shown most fully, and to the Spirit, who will make Jesus's words known to the disciples (14:26; 16:13-15, 25).

decisions.choice: the purpose of making the name known: that the Father's love for the Son, and the Son himself, may be in the disciples
decisions.reason: Knowing the Father is not only knowing about him. The love with which the Father has loved the Son (3:35; 17:24) is to live in the disciples, and so is the Son himself. The prayer ends with "and I in them", the promise of 14:20 and 14:23 and of the vine and the branches (15:4-5).

decisions.choice: and I in them (L, B), and I myself will be in them (R): last at every level
alternatives: and that I may be in them
decisions.reason: The prayer ends on the words "and I in them", which Literal and Balanced keep as the Greek has them, without a verb; the Greek leaves no other natural wording for these closing words. Readable supplies the verb but keeps the clause last, so that the prayer still ends with Jesus in them.

decisions.choice: even though ... has never known ... have known ... have come to know (B); does not know, know (R); these disciples (B, R); go on making it known, keep on doing it (B, R); the love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have had for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} (B), the love {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} have for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} (R)
decisions.reason: The aorist "knew" sums up a whole history (meaning decision m2), so Balanced uses the English perfect and Readable the plain present. Balanced says "even though" for the contrast marked by "and ... but". Balanced and Readable name "these" as the disciples, and say "go on making it known" for the future "will make known". Readable also explains "your name" as "who you are" (meaning decision m4). For "the love with which you loved me" Balanced says "the love you have had for me" and Readable "the love you have for me", since that love did not end (17:24).
